FED’S NEW ROUND OF QE FAILS TO IGNITE FURTHER 
METALS RALLY
The US Federal Reserve announced a new round of 
monetary stimulus on December 12th, committing to buy 
$45 billion per month in longer-term Treasuries on top 
of the $40 billion per month already in place to purchase 
mortgage-backed bonds.  The Fed also indicated that 
interest rates would remain near zero until unemployment 
falls to at least 6.5%.  A caveat to this was that inflation 
should not exceed 2.5% and that inflation expectations 
are contained.  However, the new measures were simply 
replacing the expiring “Operation Twist” programme, 
whereby the Fed bought an identical amount of Treasuries 
but paid for them with the proceeds from sales and 
redemptions of short-term debt.  The new purchases will 
be funded with an expansion of its $2.8 trillion balance 
sheet.  Given the latest US unemployment rate of 7.7%, 
this suggests there will be some time to go before the Fed 
will need to think about raising rates, and indeed its own 
forecasts suggest a timeline stretching into late 2015.
Although the Fed extended the monthly amount of its 
QE programme, market action suggested that this was 
already built into expectations as prices failed to react.  In 
fact, metals prices turned downwards subsequently as 
the increasing likelihood that the US would drop off the 
“fiscal cliff” loomed large.  Another dampener was the 
Fed’s downgrade to its US economic outlook, seeing GDP 
growth of between 2.3-3.0% in 2013, down from 2.5-3.0% 
in September.  The wider market is even more pessimistic.  
Adding to this is continued uncertainty over European 
debt and the region’s economic growth prospects over the 
coming year.  
Despite the trials and tribulations faced by the global 
economy this year, we are currently in a position where 
metals markets seem to have largely shrugged this off; at 
least if we judge them by price performance.  Of the LME 
base metals, the star performer through December 13th 
was tin, which gained 19.7% for the year-to-date.  This was 
followed by the two “ugly sisters” of lead and zinc, which 
gained 12.8% and 12.0%, respectively.  In zinc’s case, this 
has been in spite of the poor fundamentals and rising 
stocks faced by the metal.  Copper was next up, adding 
5.8%; perhaps its enhanced macro credentials hampered 
its upside potential relative to some of its other smaller, 
less liquid, counterparts?  Aluminium, which continues 
to be dogged by ever-increasing global (and particularly 
Chinese) output and record high LME inventories, was 
the second-worst performer on the complex, but still 
gained 4.8%.  Nickel was the stand-out; its fundamentals 
have certainly not been outstanding by any means, as 
production has outpaced consumption (especially as the 
stainless steel market has remained weak), but it was the 
only base metal to record a price fall for the year-to-date.  
The metal’s price fell 5.7% through December 13th.
Average prices for base metals for the year-to-date, with 
only a couple of weeks of trading left, are: $7,951 for copper 
(on a cash basis) – we currently forecast average 2013 
prices of $8,190/tonne; $2,016/tonne for aluminium – 
forecast for 2013 of $2,020/tonne; Nickel $17,532/tonne 
– forecast of $18,710/tonne; Zinc $1,942/tonne – forecast 
of $2,080/tonne; Lead $2,050/tonne – forecast of $2,265/
tonne; Tin $20,992/tonne – forecast of $23,965/tonne.

Economic Indicators
Revised OECD Leading Indicators show that the overall 
composite index has remained stable at 100.2 since 
July.  The overall indicator for the Eurozone slid to 99.3 
in October, from 99.4 in the previous month, whilst 
the measure for Japan was unchanged at 100.2.  More 
positively, the US indicator rose to 100.9, from 100.8 in 
September.  Elsewhere, the Chinese indicator picked up to 
99.6 after holding at 99.5 over April-September, while that 
for India also rose, to 97.3, stemming the downtrend seen 
over prior months.
The Eurozone economy shrank for the second consecutive 
quarter in the three months to September, constrained 
by weak government spending and business investment.  
Reflecting ongoing weakness, industrial output slid 1.4% 
month-on-month in October, the second consecutive 
month of decline, which included a 2.6% decline in 
Germany.  In annual terms, EU IP contracted by 3.6%, 
after shrinking by a revised 2.8% in September.  More 
positively, more recent data showed that the business and 
consumer confidence index rose for the first time in nine 
months in November to 85.7, from a three-year low of 
84.3 in October, whilst the manufacturing PMI rose for the 
second consecutive month in December to 46.3, from 46.2 
in November.  However, the PMI remained in contractionary 
territory and, despite the recent upturn in some indicators, 
we remain cautious about the extent and sustainability 
of any recovery given weak underlying activity and high 
unemployment, amongst other factors.  
Meanwhile, in Japan, conditions remain downbeat.  The 
Japanese economy shrank by an annualised 3.5% in the 
third quarter, as falling exports (weakness in Europe 
was a major factor) and the territorial dispute with China 
restricted capital expenditure, whilst the conclusion of 
some government subsidies dented consumer spending.  
Although industrial production did improve 1.8% 
month-on-month in October, it was down 4.3% year-
on-year.  Furthermore, and more recently, consumer 
confidence continued to slide to 39.0 in November, from 
39.8 in October.  The Tankan Survey also reflected the 
deterioration in sentiment; the headline diffusion index for 
large manufacturers fell from -3 in the September quarter 
to -12 in the final quarter.  Meanwhile, the manufacturing 
PMI fell to a 19-month low of 46.5 in November, from 46.9 
in the previous month.  
In the United States, GDP growth improved in the third 
quarter, rising 2.7% on an annualised basis, up from 1.3% 
in the June quarter.  Since then, trends in key indicators 
have been somewhat skewed by the disruption caused 
by Hurricane Sandy; IP rebounded 1.1% in November, 
following a revised 0.7% drop in October.  Meanwhile, 
the ISM Manufacturing PMI in November registered a 
surprise fall, to 49.5 from 51.7 in October.  More positively, 
November US consumer confidence rose for the third 
consecutive month to 73.7 from 73.1 in October, buoyed by 
the improvements in job growth over recent months. 
Finally, the latest data have supported our expectations 
for a fourth quarter rebound in the Chinese economy.  
Industrial production growth accelerated to 10.1% year-
on-year in November, from 9.6% in October, and was 
notably higher than the recent low of 8.9% recorded 
in August.  Also, the growth in fixed asset investment 
picked up to 20.7% in both October and November, from 
20.2% in September, as policy-induced infrastructure 
investment began to ramp up.  Elsewhere, an improvement 
in consumer confidence over recent months contributed 
to an acceleration in retail sales growth to 14.9% in 
November, from a low of 13.1% in July.  Finally, the Chinese 
Manufacturing PMI rose to a 14-month high of 50.9 in 
December, from 50.5 in November, driven by a resurgence 
in domestic demand.

ALUMINIUM
recent developments
• 
As the prospects for more quantitative easing grew, 
prices staged a rally through into early December.  Increasing 
optimism over Chinese growth added to this upward trend, 
although more recently the US “fiscal cliff” and Eurozone 
worries have arrested any further rises.  Recent additional 
QE announced by the Fed failed to spur another rally.  
Nevertheless, current aluminium prices are around 6% higher 
than at the end of 2011.
• 
LME stocks of aluminium registered yet another record 
high on November 29th, of 5.207 million tonnes.  Vlissingen, 
in particular, has seen a notable net influx of metal.  
Aluminium inventories on the Shanghai Exchange also 
continued to build through November.  The latest data for IAI 
unwrought stocks held by producers and aluminium held at 
major Japanese ports both showed declines in October.  Total 
reported stocks have added 355,000 tonnes (5.2%) for the 
year-to-date.
• 
Following last month’s halt to the ongoing rise in physical 
premiums, this month saw European and Japanese quotes 
flatline, whilst US premiums eased slightly.  Indications for 
first quarter Japanese term contracts are indicated in a lower 
range than for Q4.  However, reports for premiums discussed 
for 2013 generally do not show any signs of any sharp 
turnaround.
• 
The global primary production rate remained steady 
in October, supported by ongoing robust Chinese output.  
Demand, meanwhile, continues to be driven by China and the 
United States, although Europe and now Japan are acting as 
a drag on consumption growth.
outlook for the next twelve months
• 
The rally in markets seen through early December has led 
us to revise higher our forecast for the fourth quarter average.  
We now expect this to be $2,000/tonne, and the 2012 average 
cash price to realise $2,018/tonne.  The continued strength 
in global primary production, combined with the overall 
lacklustre demand environment, leads us to project market 
surpluses of 660,000 tonnes this year and 456,000 tonnes in 
2013.  
• 
Whilst we continue to feel that monetary and fiscal 
stimulus will help to support markets going into 2013, the 
scope for any significant rallies, especially in the case of 
aluminium, remains limited.  We are currently anticipating an 
average price of $2,125/tonne in the first quarter of next year 
and an annual average price in 2013 of $2,069/tonne.

December 2012 - aluminium
Market background
Prices continued the bounce seen since the end of October, 
as expectations for further quantitative easing increased.  
Allied to this has been rising optimism over Chinese 
growth, as the new regime has come in and the economy 
looks to have bottomed out in Q3.  The cash aluminium 
price peaked in its recent run-up at $2,141/tonne, but has 
since slipped back slightly.  Current levels still represent 
around a 6% increase over the year-to-date.   Despite the 
announcement on Wednesday 12th December of further 
QE measures by the Fed and the formal linkage of low 
interest rates to unemployment, markets failed to gain 
further traction.  This suggests that not only was further QE 
already factored into prevailing prices, but that concerns 
remain over Europe and a resolution to the US “fiscal cliff”.
Another new high for LME stocks
LME aluminium stocks have continued to build, as 
cancelled warrants have fallen in relative and absolute 
terms.  Having reached a new peak of 5.207 million tonnes 
on November 29th, inventories have eased since, to 5.159 
million tonnes at the time of writing.  Of the dominant 
locations of Vlissingen and Detroit, the former had a net 
influx of about 45,000 tonnes since our last report, while 
the latter location saw a fall of around 37,000 tonnes.  
Stocks on the Shanghai exchange added 19,000 tonnes 
in November and are currently only slightly lower than 
month-end, at 462,929 tonnes.  
Figures from the International Aluminium Institute (IAI) 
show that in October, total unwrought inventories of metal 
fell 18,000 tonnes from the previous month, to 1.298 
million.  Although inventories in Africa and Oceania saw 
sharp increases, of 34,000 tonnes and 22,000 tonnes, 
respectively, these were more than offset by declines 
elsewhere.  Europe and North America, in particular, 
experienced sharp declines, of 46,000 tonnes and 32,000 
tonnes, respectively; these tally with the pattern of LME 
stock increases that we saw subsequently.  Stocks of 
aluminium reported at major Japanese ports at end-
November amounted to 272,800 tonnes, up 15,000 tonnes 
on the previous month.  Total reported stocks have, since 
the beginning of the year, gained just over 355,000 tonnes, 
or 5.2%.
Premiums find further gains difficult, but no significant 
turnaround in sight yet 
Premiums have held largely steady for another month, 
even as the amount of metal in LME warehouses increases.  
This partially reflects an ongoing reluctance by consumers 
to purchase much more than immediate or nearby 
requirements.  However, recent indications for premiums 
into 2013 suggest that there are no prospects of any 
substantial discounts currently on the horizon.
US Midwest premiums for P1020 material continue to 
creep lower, with recent quotes indicated between 10.75-
11.25¢/lb, up to 0.25¢/lb lower than last month’s quotes.

recent developments
• 
Prices have rallied over recent weeks, assisted by positive 
Chinese data and expectations for (and the subsequent 
announcement of) further quantitative easing in the United 
States.  However, concerns over the US “fiscal cliff” and the 
health of the Eurozone economies continue to constrain the

• 
Third quarter reports from a number of the major 
producers implied much improved performance through the 
latter part of 2012.  Chilean mine output picked up, albeit 
at a slower rate than we anticipated, whilst the second half 
increase in Peruvian output looks like exceeding expectations. 
Meanwhile, early settlements at a number of key operations, 
including Chuquicamata and Escondida, have eased some of 
the concerns surrounding potential labour disputes.
• 
Recent data emanating from China have supported our 
expectations for a fourth quarter rebound in consumption 
there.  Nevertheless, it is clear that the country is transitioning 
to a lower rate of metals demand growth and, also taking 
into account wider concerns surrounding growth within 
key trading partners, we have reduced our expectations for 
Chinese demand growth both this year and next.  Reflecting 
the sluggishness of global growth, we have also made 
downward revisions to our forecasts for a host of other key 
consumers, including the EU-27, Japan, Russia, South Korea 
and Taiwan.
outlook for the next twelve months
• 
 We have revised our global demand and production 
forecasts lower for this report, although the key themes of 
our analysis nevertheless remain similar to our previous 
expectations.  Indeed, we continue to forecast a largely 
balanced market this year and a move to modest surplus next 
year, of 155,000 tonnes.   
•

of our last report, we have upwardly revised our fourth 
quarter price projections marginally to $7,930/tonne (from

average of $7,955/tonne.
•

in underpinning growth in key economies.  However, an 
acceleration in global production growth and the market 
oversupply are expected to cap the extent of the price upside.

December 2012 - copper
Market background
Copper prices have rallied over recent weeks, after falling 
to a low of $7,540/tonne on 9th November.  Signs of an 
improvement in the Chinese economy and expectations 
for further quantitative easing in the United States have 
been key contributors to this upward trend, helping 
copper prices to a cash official high of $8,111/tonne on 
10th December.  Reflecting the improvement in sentiment, 
investors switched to a net long position in the week 
ending 4th December (according to the CFTC managed 
money category) for the first time in four weeks.
More recently, although the Fed did indeed commit to 
further quantitative easing at the recent FOMC meeting in 
mid-December, such a development was largely priced in 
by the time of the announcement and concerns over the 
impending “fiscal cliff” have continued to weigh on the 
market.  As a result, prices have failed to build on earlier 
gains and were trading at just over $8,000/tonne at the 
time of writing.
Mine output picks up pace, whilst strike threats dissipate 
(for now)
Third quarter reports from many of the major producers 
pointed to much improved performance through the latter 
half of 2012.  Thomson Reuters GFMS expects most of the 
world’s top ten copper producers to deliver more copper in 
the remainder of the year, with global mine output forecast 
to rise 5.0% in the second half from the first half.  For the 
full year, our revised projections show output growing by 
2.0%, or 325,000 tonnes, in 2012 and by a further 4.9%, or 
801,000 tonnes, next year.
Moreover, recent concerns over the plethora of labour 
contract expiries up for renewal in late 2012 and 2013 
have dissipated somewhat in light of the early settlements 
and talks at a number of key operations, including 
Chuquicamata and Escondida.  Even so, a degree of 
nervousness will inevitably remain, particularly given that 
negotiations are due in September 2013 at Grasberg.  The 
lengthy strike there is still etched firmly on the industry’s

According to our latest forecasts, Asian output will increase 
by 4.1% this year, followed by a 12.7% rise next year as 
Indonesian output recovers.  Freeport’s Grasberg mine 
in Indonesia began ramping up in late December 2011, 
following a three-month strike, but is still only expected to 
produce 360,000 tonnes this year, less than half annual 
output achieved three years ago. However, levels will pick 
up from next year with the completion of underground 
development activities. 
The Oyu Tolgoi project in Mongolia will also make a 
sizeable contribution next year.  Meanwhile, Chinese mine 
production looks set to exceed 1.5 million tonnes this year, 
as numerous marginal operations continue to respond to 
an extended period of high prices and majors embark on 
expansion drives.
African copper mine output, meanwhile, will continue its 
recent uptrend, but a degree of caution remains in light of 
the sensitivities around access to power and wages that 
come with developing in the African Copperbelt. 
Refined output on the rise
The recent recovery in copper mine output has recently 
provided a boost to global refined production, and we 
expect this trend to continue next year.  Indeed, although 
lower scrap supply (resulting from lower prices and 
lacklustre industrial output in key economies) will continue 
in 2013, greater concentrate availability will lead to a step 
up in global refined output growth to 3.8% next year, from 
1.9% this year.  We expect refined production to reach 
20.789 million tonnes in 2013, up from 20.025 million 
tonnes in 2012.
Asia, and in particular China, will continue to account for 
the bulk of the growth as new capacity comes on stream. 
According to the latest CNIA data China produced 4.94 
million tonnes of refined copper in the first ten months 
of the year, up 7.4% from the same period last year.  We 
currently expect output for the year as a whole to rise by 
6.8%.
Refined production in Latin America is forecast to grow 
by 7.7% next year, after a disappointing 2012, during 
which time Chilean output is expected to fall by around 
6% to 2.9 million tonnes.  Meanwhile, we expect African 
production to record double-digit growth next year, helped 
by the ramp-up of production at Kansanshi and the start 
of cathode output at China Non-Ferrous Metals Corp’s 
Muliashi project.
Demand forecasts scaled back
We have lowered our demand forecasts in this report.  Our 
new projections show global consumption growing by 1.3% 
this year, from 2.4% previously.  Next year, although we 
continue to expect that demand growth will rebound from 
the 2012 low, we have moderated the rate of increase to 
3.1%, from 3.5% previously.  Our 2013 forecast now stands 
at 20.634 million tonnes, which is 1.7% lower than our 
previous forecast. 
The downgrade to our forecasts for this year is in part due 
to a slower than expected rebound in Chinese demand 
over recent months.  Consequently, as we pre-warned in 
our last report, we have reduced our growth forecast for 
that country to 4.9%, from 5.1% previously.  However, as 
we detail in the Economic Indicators section of this report, 
there have been more recent signs that the economy 
has bottomed out.  As a result, we continue to forecast 
a rebound in Chinese demand over 2013, to 5.8%, and 
this should help to eat in to mountain of stocks that have 
accumulated in bonded warehouses in recent months.

next year for news of possible smelter restarts.  Recent 
local reports in Peru suggest that Doe Run Peru’s La 
Oroya polymetallic complex, which has been shut since 
2009, began test production of zinc in July and of lead 
more recently.  It is unlikely that the plant would be able 
to operate at full capacity of 120,000 tonnes per year 
of refined lead, but, given that it had previously been 
omitted from forecasts, a restart, having previously seemed 
unlikely, could see our market deficit diminish, ceteris 
paribus. 
There has also been a recent resurgence in speculation that 
Glencore may restart its 80,000 tonne per year Portovesme 
smelter in Sardinia, which has been shut since around 
mid-2009. Rumours initially circulated last year that the 
facility would restart in September 2011, but union sources 
subsequently said re-opening had been delayed to end-
2012 to resolve environmental and technical issues. Latest 
market talk suggests a restart may be fairly imminent.
China still key driver for mine output
Global lead mine output in the first nine months of 2012 
totalled 3.923 million tonnes, up 563,000 tonnes or 16.8% 
from year-ago levels, according to the ILZSG.  
China accounted for by far the greatest part of that rise, 
with output there jumping 31.7% to 2.130 million tonnes, 
ILZSG figures showed.  The latest CNIA figures indicate a 
considerably slower, but still substantial, pace of growth. 
In the first ten months they suggest growth of around 20% 
year-on-year.
Outside China, year-on-year changes in mine output have 
been pretty small on the whole. The most significant 
increases were in fourth largest producer Peru (+21,000 
tonnes) and fifth largest Mexico (+20,000 tonnes). The 
increase in Mexican output is due largely to higher output 
from Goldcorp’s Penasquito mine, despite water shortages 
there.
In Australia, the second largest producer of mined lead, 
output was down 10,000 tonnes year-on-year in January 
to September, according to the ILZSG.  As we noted last 
month, third quarter results from key Australian operations 
showed mixed performances over the period. 
Looking ahead to next year, we assume that Ivernia will be 
in a position to restart production at its Paroo Station mine 
(formerly Magellan) in Western Australia in the second 
quarter.  Operations have been suspended for nearly two 
years following concerns about lead contamination.  When 
fully operational, the mine is expected to produce 85,000 
tonnes per year of contained lead.  Its concentrates would 
be destined for Chinese smelters.
Lead demand supported by Chinese offtake
Global lead demand rose by 3.2% over the opening nine 
months of the year, to 7.940 million tonnes, the latest 
statistics from the ILZSG showed.  China was the largest 
contributor to growth, with offtake there rising by 201,000 
tonnes (+6.0%).  
Chinese lead demand has been supported by a surge in 
lead-acid battery production, with data from the National 
Bureau of Statistics showing cumulative output over the 
January-October period up 28.9% year-on-year.  However, 
demand for such batteries has reportedly failed to keep 
pace and, as such, inventories have been on the rise.

December 2012 - lead
Further downstream, and more recently, the growth in auto 
production rebounded in November to 3.9% year-on-year, 
supporting demand for original equipment batteries.  This 
represented an improvement on the 1.1% year-on-year 
increase seen in October, although remained below the 
cumulative growth figure of 4.5% that was seen over the 
first eleven months.  The territorial dispute with Japan, 
which cut demand for Japanese cars and led Japanese 
automakers to slash production within China, has in part 
been accountable for the slowdown in growth over recent 
months.
Outside of China, consumption rose by just 50,000 
tonnes, or 1.1%.  Increases in India (+30,000 tonnes), 
Mexico (+15,000 tonnes), Turkey (+11,000 tonnes) and the 
United States (+15,000 tonnes) were offset by declines 
in Indonesia (-13,000 tonnes) and a host of European 
countries, including France (-12,000 tonnes), Italy (-10,000 
tonnes) and Poland (-14,000 tonnes).
Market outlook
With price forecasts largely performing in line with our 
expectations, our fourth quarter price projection remains 
unchanged from our previous report, at $2,195/tonne.  This 
would give a full year 2012 average of $2,060/tonne, down 
14.1% year-on-year.
Our longer term forecasts also remain unchanged from our 
previous report and, under our base case scenario, lead 
prices are forecast to rise 9.5% year-on-year to $2,255/
tonne.  An improvement in the economic environment 
would be a key precondition to such a price improvement, 
driving demand from both investors and consumers.  
Specifically, we expect underlying lead demand to rise by 
6.3% in 2013.  Consequently, despite also stimulating a 
supply response, we would expect the market to move into 
deficit in 2013 for the first time in four years, albeit at a 
relatively small 51,000 tonnes.
A sharper than expected recovery in the economic 
environment would lead demand higher than our base 
case forecasts and place pressure on metal availability.  
Under this scenario, dubbed our high case scenario B, 
we forecast average prices of $2,550/tonne next year.  In 
contrast, our low case scenario C would see prices average 
$1,840/tonne in 2013.  Lower than expected demand 
growth would be the key precondition to such a scenario 
materialising.

December 2012 - nickel & cobalt
Market background
Growing anticipation of further quantitative easing and a 
brighter outlook for China’s economy, which looks to have 
bottomed out in the third quarter, helped metal markets 
to post gains into early December.  Nickel cash prices 
peaked recently at $17,759/tonne, although had fallen 
back to around $17,428/tonne at the time of writing.  This 
was despite the Fed’s announcement of further QE and 
clarification of its low interest rate stance and the link with 
unemployment.  Market expectations of QE looked like they 
had already been built into the preceding price rise, whilst 
worries over a speedy resolution to the US “fiscal cliff” 
negotiations combined with ongoing concerns regarding 
Europe’s economic shape.  Stainless steel markets, 
meanwhile, remain lacklustre.
European nickel and stainless markets remain especially 
weak
In comparison to the INSG demand numbers highlighted 
last month, the WBMS estimates that global refined nickel 
consumption during January-September increased by 
6.1% (74,000 tonnes); the INSG’s figure was 2.1% growth 
(25,200 tonnes).  According to the WBMS, over the first 
nine months, the major increases to consumption (in 
volume terms) came from China (+17.0%, 84,900 tonnes 
year-on-year), South Korea (+15.6%, 11,100 tonnes) and 
India (+29.2%, 5,500 tonnes).  The main losses to demand 
were seen in Japan (-11.3%, 15,100 tonnes), Belgium 
(-37.1%, 8,600 tonnes) and Sweden (-22.5%, 5,300 
tonnes).
The improved nickel price environment has encouraged 
many stainless steel producers in Asia to roll-over, or in 
some cases raise, prices in December.  There were some 
exceptions; in Foshan’s spot market in south China for 
example, stainless coil prices were reported to have 
remained steady at best and were softer for some grades.
Taiwan’s largest stainless producer, Yieh United Steel Corp 
(Yusco) had said at end-November that it was rolling over 
its export prices, although reports indicated that it may 
have raised some prices.  Meanwhile, Taiwanese producer 
Tang Eng Iron Works rolled-over its 300-series stainless 
steel hot rolled and cold rolled coil prices for December 
for both domestic and overseas sales.  Nippon Steel & 
Sumikin Stainless (NSSC) also held its domestic prices for 
cold rolled stainless coil and plate for December contracts, 
citing lower nickel prices.  China’s Taigang Stainless Steel 
and Baosteel both cut their 300-series stainless HRC and 
CRC export prices by $50/tonne for December.
South Korea’s Posco, however, kept its prices steady, which 
was reported to be making its material relatively attractive 
to buyers.  Recently, the Posco Research Institute forecast 
that Korea’s total output of stainless HRC in 2013 would 
increase by 9% year-on-year to 2.04 million tonnes, on the 
back of a modest recovery in domestic demand and decent 
export growth. Stainless CRC production was anticipated 
to rise by 2% year-on-year to 1.13 million tonnes.

December 2012 - nickel & cobalt
The spot physical nickel market in Europe has slowed 
as prices have risen, and more attention appears to be 
focused on next year.  However, the lower price range 
through much of November has led to European stainless 
steel surcharges for December being lowered.  All four 
major European stainless steel producers - Acerinox, 
ThyssenKrupp, Aperam and Outokumpu - dropped alloy 
surcharges for various 300- and 400-series grades for 
December production. In the United States, ThyssenKrupp 
Stainless USA was reported to have eased most of its 
300-series stainless surcharges for December, on the back 
of previously lower nickel prices.  However, ferritic material 
surcharges showed some gains.
European stainless steel distributor, Damstahl, recently 
reported that the stainless steel market in Europe is 
not showing any signs of improvement at the moment.  
Demand from both end-users and stockholders lacked 
any clear direction.  Although raw material price rises in 
December are too late to prompt any significant stocking, 
the company expects distributors to be back in the market 
in the first quarter of 2013.  However, Damstahl expects 
that end-use demand will remain flat over the next 
few months, at least, and that even in the longer term, 
the European stainless steel market will not show any 
volume growth, with Italy posing the biggest downside 
risk.  However, the second half of next year is expected to 
be better than the first, with the oil & gas sector being a 
particular bright spot.
Ups and downs in output
It has been a rather mixed month for nickel production.  
Underlining the general uptrend in supply that remains in 
place, Xstrata recently announced that it had completed 
construction of the first production line at its 60,000 tpy 
Koniambo ferro-nickel project in New Caledonia.  The 
company anticipates first metal production from January 
2013.  The recent start-up of the Ramu project in Papua 
New Guinea also looks to be running smoothly.  Highlands 
Pacific said it had loaded its maiden shipment of mixed 
nickel-cobalt hydroxide intermediate product.
On the other side of the equation, though, Talvivaara’s 
Sotkamo mine in Finland has continued to experience 
difficulties.  The firm, which has been hit by a series of 
problems in the past year, including waste water leakage 
and production disruptions, recently postponed the restart 
of mining by six months because of rain-related issues.  
Talvivaara now expects to produce 13,000 tonnes of nickel 
this year, and said production might not pick up much next 
year, nor possibly even in 2014.  At full capacity, Sotkamo 
should be able to produce a significantly higher 50,000 
tpy.
Despite the persistent problems at Sotkamo and losses in 
Brazil and Venezuela, which were covered in last month’s 
report, global refined nickel production still looks set to 
grow at a pretty robust pace next year, underpinned by 
contributions from new projects and Chinese NPI plants.
Nickel ore exports from Indonesia are expected to surge 
next year as producers maximise shipments ahead of a 
law banning shipments of unprocessed raw materials 
from 2014.  Indonesia’s PT Aneka Tambang said it hoped 
to double its nickel ore production next year to as much as 
18.8 million tonnes ahead of the ban.  Higher Indonesian 
ore exports will likely feed through into higher Chinese 
NPI supply, even though many NPI plants reportedly are 
running at reduced rates at present due to modest demand 
from stainless steel producers.   The growing proportion 
of lower-cost NPI capacity in China also means nickel 
prices would have to fall a lot further than the previous 
oft-cited $17,000/tonne threshold before cutbacks on any 
significant scale kick in.

projects has re-surfaced.  In late November, Nickel Asia 
said the cost of building the second processing plant at 
its Taganito HPAL operation in the Philippines had risen

Vale said Goro can make an operating profit, but it is not

recent developments
• 
LME spot tin prices averaged $20,700/tonne in 
November, 3% lower than the October average.  Prices started

eight-month high of $23,155/tonne on 12th December.  
• 
Global tin supply remains under pressure.  Mine output 
in a number of major producing countries declined over the 
first nine months of the year, the latest data from the WBMS 
showed. 
• 
Chinese mine production continued to fall in October, 
down 21% year-on-year to 5,862 tonnes.  China’s refined 
output also declined at a similar pace, falling 20% year-on-
year in the corresponding month to 12,781 tonnes. 
• 
Indonesia, the world’s largest tin exporter, saw its 
November shipments decline 28% month-on-month to 7,946 
tonnes.  From January to November, Indonesia exported a 
total of 90,127 tonnes of refined tin, up 11% compared to the 
same period of last year.  We believe that this overstates the 
strength of Indonesian output, with the ongoing depletion 
of easily-accessed mines continuing to weigh on the 
performance of the country’s producers. 
• 
Demand from the top consumer China remains subdued, 
with refined tin imports into the country declining by 30% 
month-on-month in October.  Moving towards the year 
end, domestic demand for electronic products has showed 
some strength, although this has been largely offset by the 
weakness in export orders.
outlook for the next twelve months
• 
Thomson Reuters GFMS continue to hold a bullish view 
on the tin market.  The global market is expected to be in a 
10,000 tonne deficit next year, after recording a shortfall of 
11,000 tonnes this year.
• 
The ongoing issues in the mining industry remain the 
focal point in the tin market, and the resulting tightness in 
supply will continue to provide momentum to prices in the 
coming year.  Downside risks to our price forecasts mainly 
come from the demand side, as sluggish global growth 
continues to constrain offtake.  
• 
Our base case scenario assumes an improvement in the 
global economic environment next year and, given tin’s strong 
fundamental backdrop, the market would be poised for a 
rally.  Consequently, under our base case scenario, we expect 
tin prices to average $23,965/tonne in 2013, up 14% from the 
expected average of $21,020/tonne this year.

Market background
Tin prices regained strength in early December, after 
ending November with a monthly average of $20,700/

contributed by a renewed round of buying interest in the tin

Refined tin inventories held at LME warehouses have

December, fluctuating around 12,000 tonnes.  On-warrant

the year, down 12% from 228,200 tonnes over the same 
period last year.  More than half of the decline came from 
China during this period, with domestic tin-in-concentrate 
production down by 16,900 tonnes to 82,100 tonnes, 
according to the WBMS.  Outside of China, declines were 
mainly seen in Peru (-2,300 tonnes), the Democratic 
Republic of Congo (-1,600 tonnes) and Bolivia (-900 
tonnes).  In terms of refined production, global refined

September, 7% lower than the production over the same
